title: Rotation and Angular Momentum

cards.b:
A skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. A cat falls upside down and lands on its feet. A spinning top stands up when it should fall. A bicycle stays upright because its wheels spin.

These all come from the physics of rotation. It mirrors the physics of straight-line motion, with new names: torque instead of force, moment of inertia instead of mass, angular momentum instead of momentum.

We measure angles in radians: one full turn is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians. Angular velocity (omega) is how many radians per second. A wheel making one turn per second has omega = 6.28 rad/s.

A point at distance r from the axis moves with speed v = r x omega. So the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub, though both turn together.

cards.h: Torque: the twist of a force
cards.b:
Torque

torque = force x perpendicular distance from the axis

You open a door by pushing far from the hinges, not near them. Same force, longer lever arm, more torque. A long spanner loosens a tight nut for the same reason.

Archimedes is said to have boasted that with a long enough lever he could move the Earth. Torque is the principle behind it.

Mass resists a change in straight-line motion. Moment of inertia (I) resists a change in spin. It depends on how the mass is spread: mass far from the axis counts much more.

Rotational second law

torque = I x angular acceleration

For a point mass, I = m r squared. A solid disc spins up more easily than a ring of the same mass, because the ring has all its mass at the edge.

Angular momentum

L = I x omega

If no outside torque acts, L stays constant. A skater spinning with arms out has a large I. Pulling arms in cuts I, so omega must rise to keep L the same.

This is why a collapsing star spins faster as it shrinks, producing the rapidly spinning neutron stars we call pulsars.

cards.h: Rolling and the kinetic energy of spin
cards.b:
A rolling wheel has two energies: motion of its centre, (1/2) m v squared, and spin, (1/2) I omega squared. On a slope, a solid ball beats a hollow ring in a race, because less of its energy goes into spin.

This also explains why a gyroscope or spinning top resists tilting: its angular momentum wants to stay pointing the same way. Gyroscopes guide aircraft and ships.

A skater spins at 2 rad/s with I = 4 kg m squared. She pulls her arms in so I = 1 kg m squared.

Conservation: I1 x omega1 = I2 x omega2, so 4 x 2 = 1 x omega2, giving omega2 = 8 rad/s, four times faster.

Her rotational energy goes from (1/2) x 4 x 4 = 8 J to (1/2) x 1 x 64 = 32 J. The extra energy comes from her muscles pulling her arms inwards.

• 'Torque is just force.' No. It also depends on where you push. A force through the axis gives no torque at all.
  • 'Bigger mass always means bigger I.' I depends on the spread of mass, not only its amount.
  • 'Angular momentum is lost when the skater speeds up.' It stays the same; the spin rate and I trade off.

cards.h: The potter's wheel and the satellite
cards.b:
India's traditional potter's wheel, the chaak of the kumhar, is a heavy flywheel. Its large moment of inertia stores spin, so it keeps turning smoothly between pushes of the potter's stick.

Satellites, including Indian ones, often steer using spinning wheels inside them. Speeding up or slowing a wheel makes the satellite turn the other way, by conservation of angular momentum, with no fuel used.

• Torque = force x lever arm; it makes things rotate.
  • Moment of inertia I depends on how mass is spread out from the axis.
  • Angular momentum L = I omega is conserved without outside torque.
  • Pulling mass inward speeds up rotation.

2. Why does a cat twist its body and extend or retract its legs while falling?
